prize_parts.citation: for founding modern political economics by analysing how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: Persson, Tabellini and Besley turned questions about political institutions into formal models with testable predictions. These cover how electoral rules, constitutional design, accountability and state capacity affect fiscal policy, public-goods provision and economic performance. The contribution is a framework plus an empirical agenda, not a single result, and the field it created is now a standard part of public economics, development and comparative politics. Attribution is unusually clean: the Persson-Tabellini constitutional and electoral-rules program and its book-length synthesis, and Besley's work on political agency and state capacity, form one coherent body of work. The work is 25 or more years old, so there has been ample time for replication, extension and critique. After reading the openings, I keep this as my preferred case. The strongest competing cases (B003, B047, B014) are also strong, but none of the arguments raised against B032 undermines the core contribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are these. First, the 2024 institutions-and-prosperity prize makes a neighbouring topic recent. Second, some cross-country estimates of constitutional effects rest on observational variation with real identification problems. Third, B032 has the narrowest endorsement among the leading candidates, and some colleagues may judge its breadth of impact on core economics to be lower than that of the New Keynesian, collateral-constraint or heterogeneous-firm work. Fourth, I work in IO and trade, so ranking a political-economy entry first means relying on the common criteria rather than field expertise. That is a reason for humility about my own ranking, not a reason to treat colleagues' support counts as scientific evidence.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranked B032 seventh, noting that the 2024 institutions prize may reduce room for an award in a neighbouring area. He also noted Persson's Stockholm affiliation as a conflict-type factor without adjudicating it.
responses.response: The thematic overlap is real but it is not an overlap in contribution. The 2024 award concerned how colonial-era institutions shaped long-run prosperity. Persson, Tabellini and Besley explain how specific rules (electoral systems, constitutional structure, accountability mechanisms, fiscal capacity) map into policy choices within a formal framework. Different question, different method, different empirical objects. I accept that the committee may still see the topics as adjacent, and I count that as a genuine timing risk. On the Stockholm affiliation, I have no personal link to the candidates that I can see in my profile, and I agree it should be disclosed and not adjudicated.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B032 second. He flagged his own proximity to the field and acknowledged that empirical identification in the constitutional-comparison studies has been challenged. He also noted that the 2024 prize may make the committee reluctant.
responses.response: I agree on identification, and it shapes my citation: it credits the framework and the creation of a testable research program, not settled causal magnitudes for constitutional effects. I also take his proximity disclosure seriously, because the committee's ranking should not depend on familiarity. My own ranking rests on the common criteria of originality, breadth of influence and attribution clarity. I accept that a citation covering both theory and evidence is only as strong as its weakest empirical strand.

responses.point: Strömberg ranked B003 first and proposed Moore, Kiyotaki and Gertler. He argued that Gertler's financial-accelerator and intermediary work is central, and that the Bernanke link, though complicated by the 2022 prize, makes the area related but not duplicative.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is among the strongest cases on the shortlist, which is why it is my first alternative. I would resist adding Gertler. Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-author origin of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. The accelerator line overlaps with work already recognised in 2022, and Gertler is also a leading name in B014, so including him blurs both attribution and the distinctness of the award. If the committee prefers B003 to B032, I would support the pair.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B030 first (Grossman and Helpman, protection for sale and growth-and-trade). He acknowledged mixed empirical support for the protection-for-sale model and a possible overlap with the 2008 trade prize.
responses.response: I take the Grossman-Helpman partnership seriously as theory. As someone who works on trade and pricing, though, I find the firm-level empirical validation of the heterogeneous-firm framework in B047 much stronger than the mixed record he himself notes for protection for sale. If the committee wants a trade award, B047 is the better-supported case. Helpman's presence on both ballot entries means the committee should choose deliberately where his contribution is credited, not split it across two awards.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the 2024 institutions prize as crowding out a political-economy award so soon, or as evidence that the field is recognised and receptive.

How far the cross-country constitutional and electoral-rule estimates survive modern identification standards, and whether the citation should lean on theory and agenda-setting rather than on empirical magnitudes.

Whether the third name, Besley, is the right one alongside Persson and Tabellini, given his distinct state-capacity and accountability contributions, or whether the committee would prefer a narrower pair.
Whether my first-place ranking of a field outside my expertise reflects the common criteria or unrecognised familiarity bias, since it has the narrowest support on the shortlist.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-requiring connection to any shortlisted candidate is apparent from my supplied profile. For transparency, the profile records the following public facts, which I do not treat as bearing on any candidate: co-authorship with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026), and marriage to Magdalena Andersson. A colleague has noted a Stockholm affiliation for one candidate, and I am at SSE in Stockholm, but my profile shows no personal or co-authorship link to the candidates.
